title: Study Tricks That Work
objective: After this level you can explain the spacing and testing effects and why rereading works less well than it feels.
summary: Practice testing and spaced study beat rereading and cramming. Retrieving a memory strengthens it, even though restudying feels more reassuring.

cards.headline: Rereading your notes feels like studying. Research says it barely helps.
cards.body: Most students reread and highlight, yet these habits don't consistently boost performance. Two other techniques do, and the evidence for them is strong.

cards.headline: Testing beats restudying
cards.body: In a 2006 study by Roediger and Karpicke, students read prose passages, then either took recall tests or restudied the same material. Five minutes later, the restudiers did better. But two days or a week later, the tested students remembered substantially more, even though restudying made students more confident. The act of pulling a memory out makes it easier to pull out again: the testing effect.

cards.headline: Spacing beats cramming
cards.body: Distributed practice means studying in several short sessions spread over time instead of one long cram. Memory consolidation takes time, and spacing gives memories that time. Ebbinghaus ran the first study of this spacing effect, and it is arguably the most replicable finding in experimental psychology.

cards.headline: The 2013 verdict
cards.body: A 2013 review led by John Dunlosky rated ten popular study techniques. Only two earned the top rating of high utility: practice testing and distributed practice. They helped learners of different ages and abilities on many kinds of tasks. Rereading and highlighting were rated low, and the advice was blunt: use practice testing instead of rereading.

mascot.line: Every question you answer here is practice testing. Now you know why the questions come after the cards.

questions.prompt: According to research on the testing effect, how does taking a practice test help you remember?

options.label: It makes you feel more confident
options.rationale: Restudying raised confidence more, yet tested students remembered more.

options.label: Retrieving a memory makes it easier to retrieve again
It shows you the material one more time
options.rationale: That describes restudying; the benefit came from recalling.

options.label: It works best when the exam is minutes away
options.rationale: At five minutes, restudying actually did better.

questions.explanation: Pulling a memory out strengthens it. In the 2006 study, tested students remembered more after days or a week, even though restudying felt better.

questions.prompt: Ebbinghaus, who charted the forgetting curve, also ran the first study of _____.

options.label: the testing effect
options.rationale: The testing effect comes from research like Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study.

options.label: context-dependent memory
options.rationale: That's the 1975 divers study of memory and place.

options.label: chunking
options.rationale: Chunking is about packing more into working memory.

questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus ran the first study of the spacing effect: memory lasts better when learning is spread out over time.
